analysis.one_liner: Bans toxic chemicals like PFAS and phthalates from food packaging.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or floor vote in the House; it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal food law to declare several chemical classes illegal to use in food packaging: ortho-phthalates, PFAS (so-called 'forever chemicals'), bisphenols including BPA and BPS, styrene, and antimony trioxide. These chemicals are used in plastic containers, can linings, and grease-resistant wrappers, and can migrate into the food people eat. The ban would take effect two years after passage, and it would require the FDA to consider effects on infants, pregnant women, workers, and other heavily exposed groups when approving replacement chemicals. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially children and pregnant women, who would see phased-out chemicals linked to hormone disruption and other health risks removed from food packaging. Workers at packaging plants and residents of communities near manufacturing would also get explicit protection, since the bill requires regulators to consider their exposure when judging replacement chemicals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Deems eleven named ortho-phthalates, all PFAS chemicals, bisphenols A/B/S/F/AF, styrene, and antimony trioxide unsafe as food contact substances under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, taking effect two years after enactment.

Requires the FDA, when reviewing petitions for replacement packaging chemicals, to consider potential adverse effects on vulnerable populations including infants, children, pregnant women, the elderly, workers, and communities with disproportionate exposure.
Defines PFAS broadly as any man-made chemical with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom, covering the entire class rather than chemical-by-chemical review.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers that produce these additives and packaging companies that use them would face reformulation costs. Food and beverage brands would need new packaging; those costs could be passed to consumers in the short term, though substitutes exist for many uses.

drawbacks.text: The blanket class-based ban includes chemicals with very different toxicity profiles; some uses, such as certain industrial seals or specialized packaging, may lack proven drop-in substitutes, which could raise packaging costs or force workarounds.
Costs of reformulating packaging would fall on manufacturers and ultimately show up in food prices, an expense supporters would have to acknowledge even if they judge the health gains worth it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: several of these chemicals are known or suspected endocrine disruptors and the bill targets exactly the pathway where they reach people—food contact—while giving industry a two-year transition. The main cost is reformulation spending and possible short-term price effects, which are modest next to a permanent class-wide removal from the food supply. A fair objection is that a legislative list freezes chemicals in statute rather than letting FDA update it as science evolves, but the bill does require review of alternatives with attention to vulnerable groups.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on October 26, 2023, with eight original Democratic cosponsors including Reps. DeLauro, Dingell, and Grijalva.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, and on November 3, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill never attracted a Republican cosponsor; all thirteen cosponsors listed were House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical and packaging manufacturers that use PFAS, phthalates, and bisphenols in food packaging benefit, since no ban took effect and consumers continue to be exposed through food containers, can linings, and wrappers.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the No Toxics in Food Packaging Act on October 26, 2023.

for.name: 13 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed at the Health Subcommittee from November 2023 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill was sponsored by a Democrat; the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on it, and no Republican sponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would ban phthalates, PFAS, bisphenols, styrene, and antimony trioxide in food contact materials, forcing reformulation and new equipment. Because the bill died, the industry kept its existing packaging lines and markets.

industries.industry: Chemical producers of phthalates, PFAS, and bisphenols
industries.note: These firms would lose a major food-contact market under the class-wide ban, including all PFAS regardless of specific chemistry. The bill's death left those revenue streams intact.

Brands would face packaging compliance costs but also benefit from removing chemicals that regulators, states, and lawsuits have increasingly targeted. The bill's failure spared them near-term switching costs.
